How much does it cost to translate a document?

April 28, 2021
Professional Translation | Business | Outsourcing

If you are a UK business planning to sell, hire or operate in another language, one of your first questions is likely to be what translation costs. It is a fair question, and the honest answer is that no single figure applies to every document.

The price of a translation depends on what you need translated, into which language, how fast and to what standard. This page explains what drives translation costs in the UK, so you can budget with confidence and compare quotes properly.

How translation services are priced

Most providers base translation prices on the number of words in your source text, because word count is a fair measure of the work involved. Some quote per page, which is harder to compare, so ask how many words a page is assumed to hold. Specialist tasks, such as layout work or in-context review, are often charged by the hour.

At BeTranslated, rates are quoted per project. That means you receive one clear quote for the whole job, with a breakdown on request, instead of an hourly meter running in the background. Send us your document and we will give you a quote based on the factors below.

Factors in the cost to translate a document

These factors affect the cost of translating a document:

  • translation purpose
  • language combinations
  • word count and repetition
  • turnaround time
  • technical level
  • file format
  • frequency

Let us look at each one, so you know what to expect from your quote and where to build it into your budget.

Translation purpose

Ask yourself who your audience is, whether the document is internal or external, and what level of polish it needs. The answers affect the level of checking required and, consequently, the price.

Documents for public use, such as brochures or web pages, need a high standard and extra editing. Internal documents, where understanding matters more than elegant phrasing, can be more cost-effective because they need less rigorous checking.

Post-edited machine translation is another way to keep costs down for suitable content. Here, a human translator revises and edits a machine translation, which can suit large volumes of lower-risk text. Some language combinations respond better to this approach than others, and it is not suitable for contracts or other documents where an error carries risk.

Language combination

You may be wondering what it costs to translate a document into several languages at once. The answer varies, because each language combination has its own supply of qualified translators.

Rarer combinations usually cost more than popular ones such as English to Spanish, as fewer specialists work in them. Translating into several languages at once multiplies the work, although a single project manager coordinating all of them can keep the process simple.

The price also reflects the expertise of the professional native-language translators in our network.

Word count and repetition

Translation is generally priced on the number of words in the source text, so a short document costs less than a long one. Repeated sentences and matches from previous translations can sometimes be discounted, and a larger project can attract volume discounts.

Ask whether a minimum charge applies to short documents, and whether your quote includes VAT. If you are working to a tight budget, batching your content into fewer, larger projects can reduce the cost over time.

How long does a translation take?

If you need a translation quickly, expect to pay more. A fast turnaround demands more linguists and more coordination, and rushing can put consistency at risk.

Plan ahead where you can, and tell us your deadline when you ask for a quote so that we can propose a realistic schedule. Our network of translators works across time zones, so we can usually find the right linguist for your deadline.

Technical level

The more specialised a document, the higher the price tends to be. Legal contracts, medical texts and IT content, including software and user interfaces, need linguists who know the subject as well as the language.

Technical translations can also depend on the situation, so we work with our linguists to find the right terminology and involve experts from your company in the final word choice. You can provide a glossary to keep your terms consistent across every text.

What file formats can be translated?

The format of your file changes the work involved. These are the main cases:

  • CAT tools: Word and Excel files work well with translation software. Other file types may need converting first, which adds time and cost.

  • DTP tools: InDesign and Illustrator files need layout editing once the language changes, which BeTranslated offers at an additional cost.

  • ICR (in-context review): Available for translated website content and billed by the hour.

How often do you need translations?

If you have regular needs, you can usually benefit from discounts and from a translation memory. This is a database of your previous translations, so the same wording is reused for consistency and you avoid paying twice for repeated text.

It is particularly useful for content such as product catalogues. BeTranslated can create and host your translation memory and use it in every new project.

How much does a certified translation cost?

A certified translation costs more than a standard one, because the translator or agency adds a signed statement to the finished document. For documents you submit to the Home Office or another UK body, GOV.UK guidance says the translator should confirm in writing that the translation is true and accurate, with the date, their full name and their contact details.

Some organisations ask for more, such as notarisation, so check with the body that will receive your document before you order. Then tell us exactly what it requires when you request your quote. Our document translation team handles personal, business and legal documents.

How to keep translation costs under control

  • Finish and approve your source text before you send it, as changes mid-project cost time.
  • Supply editable files rather than scans or images of text.
  • Share a glossary, style guide and earlier translations.
  • Group related documents into one project.
  • Leave enough time to avoid a rush fee.

What to check in a translation quote

When you compare quotes, make sure each one covers the same scope. Check the word count used, the languages, whether a second linguist reviews the translation, how formatting is handled, the delivery date, whether VAT is included and what happens if you need changes. A lower price may leave out a review step that protects your reputation.

Your perfect translation

Now that you know what drives translation costs, you can decide on the right option for your business and your budget. At BeTranslated, we help you control costs so that your translated content suits its purpose and audience.

For a clear price, send us your document through our quote request page. You can also see how we work on our rates page, or call us on +442030269848 or email hello@betranslated.co.uk for a free, no-obligation quote.

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to translate a document?

The cost depends on the word count, language combination, subject, file format and deadline. We quote per project, so send your document and you will receive a clear quote.

Do translators charge per word or per page?

Many translators and agencies charge per source word, while some quote per page. If a provider quotes per page, ask how many words it counts as a page so you can compare quotes fairly.

How much does a certified translation cost?

The cost is based on the same factors as any translation, plus the certification statement from the translator or agency. Tell us which organisation will receive the document, and we will quote for the level of certification it requires.

Why does a rush translation cost more?

A tight deadline means more translators, more coordination and less time for review. Planning ahead, or splitting a large project into stages, helps you avoid paying for urgency.

How can you reduce translation costs?

Send final, editable source files, share a glossary and keep related work together in one project. Repeated text and a translation memory can also reduce the cost of regular work.
